Catch threats before they escalate with real-time Identity Telemetry

Sponsored by tenfold Software, the article promotes its no-code identity governance platform, which adds real-time Windows and Active Directory event auditing to help organizations detect suspicious identity activity and investigate it with access context.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The sponsored article argues that periodic access reviews and role-based access rules alone do not provide enough protection against modern identity-focused threats.
  • 02tenfold says its platform collects Windows and Active Directory event logs in real time, adds context such as the user associated with a session ID, and combines related multi-step events into one entry.
  • 03The platform provides searchable, shareable custom queries intended to help administrators investigate events such as privileged-account logins and password-reset requests.
  • 04tenfold combines identity governance, data access governance, and real-time event monitoring in one no-code solution.
  • 05The article states that event auditing is included in all tenfold editions, currently supports Windows and Active Directory events, and is planned to add Entra ID support and automated alerting in future releases.

The sponsored article argues that identity governance practices such as role-based access and periodic access reviews are no longer sufficient on their own against modern threats. It says organizations need real-time visibility into identity events so they can recognize when access rules are being broken and investigate possible breaches as they occur. tenfold promotes its platform as a no-code solution combining identity governance, data access governance, and real-time event monitoring.

According to the article, tenfold collects Windows and Active Directory event logs in real time, records selected event types, and adds context such as identifying the user associated with a session ID. It can consolidate related steps, such as creating and renaming a security group, into one entry, and supports searchable and shareable custom queries for events including privileged-account logins and password-reset requests. If an account appears compromised, administrators can review its access and temporarily restrict it by changing its lifecycle phase; event auditing is included in all editions, while Entra ID monitoring and automated alerts are planned for future releases.

  • The platform is designed to reduce investigation effort by linking session IDs to the user behind a change and combining related actions, such as creating and renaming a security group, into a single record.
  • An administrator who identifies a potentially compromised account can immediately view its access and change its lifecycle status to temporarily restrict the account during an investigation.
  • Although the article presents the platform as broad identity monitoring, its current event-monitoring coverage is limited to Windows and Active Directory; Entra ID monitoring and automated alerts are described as upcoming features.

This sponsored article promotes tenfold, a service that helps businesses manage who can use their systems and watch for important account changes as they happen. It says companies are adding more cloud services and outside accounts while facing more advanced scams and software attacks, making stolen or misused accounts a major risk. The product is aimed at organizations using Windows and Active Directory and can help them trace suspicious changes to a person, review what an account can access, and temporarily lock it down while they investigate.

Custom ChatGPTs push ClickFix attacks to deploy RAT malware

Malicious custom ChatGPTs promoted through Google ads are directing users to fake Cloudflare checks that use ClickFix PowerShell commands to install a remote-access trojan. The campaign uses signed application DLL sideloading and persistent Windows Registry and scheduled-task entries, with OpenAI removing at least one malicious GPT.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Threat actors promoted malicious custom ChatGPT variants in sponsored Google search results and used them to direct users to a Google Sites page posing as a backup site.
  • 02The malicious page displayed a fake Cloudflare check that instructed visitors to run a PowerShell command, which installed a malicious MSI and ultimately deployed a remote-access trojan.
  • 03The RAT can provide remote desktop access, capture audio and camera data, search files, collect host information, and run additional payloads.
  • 04The malware persists by creating both a Windows Registry Run key and a scheduled task named "Canon Configuration Reader."
  • 05Huntress investigated at least 40 incidents linked to the Google Sites page, confirmed two involving a malicious custom GPT, and reported that OpenAI removed the first GPT before a second linked GPT was found.

Threat actors promoted malicious custom ChatGPT variants in sponsored Google results and used them to direct users to a Google Sites page presented as a backup site. The page showed a fake Cloudflare check and told visitors to run a PowerShell command, a ClickFix technique that begins the malware installation chain. Huntress investigated at least 40 incidents connected to the page, though it confirmed only two that involved a custom GPT variant.

The command installs a malicious MSI that launches a legitimate signed application alongside a modified DLL carrying a remote-access trojan. The RAT can enable remote desktop access, audio and camera capture, file searches, host reconnaissance, and execution of additional payloads, while persistence is maintained through a Run key and scheduled task named “Canon Configuration Reader.” Huntress said the attackers changed from using a Canon-signed application to a Stardock-signed one while retaining the same payload, and highlighted suspicious process activity such as PowerShell silently launching an MSI from a temporary folder as a detection opportunity.

  • The campaign gains credibility by placing malicious instructions within OpenAI-hosted custom GPTs and then sending users to a purported backup site, making the scam appear to rely on familiar services.
  • Although Huntress investigated at least 40 incidents linked to the Google Sites page, it confirmed only two involving a custom GPT, indicating the same malicious destination was used through more than one route.
  • The attackers changed from a Canon-signed application to a Stardock-signed application and altered their loader concealment and delivery methods while retaining the same RAT payload.
  • The malware uses a custom encrypted file system with an index of 1,128 file and folder entries to hide its persistence script and RAT, rather than storing everything in a single encrypted file.
  • Because much of the infection chain runs in memory or relies on benign-looking files, Huntress recommends monitoring suspicious process activity, such as PowerShell invoking msiexec to silently install an MSI from a temporary folder.

Criminals created fake custom versions of ChatGPT and promoted them in Google search results, then sent people to a page that pretended to perform a security check. The page told visitors to run a command on their Windows computers, which installed software that could let attackers view the screen, use the camera or microphone, search files, and add more harmful software. Huntress investigated at least 40 visits connected to the malicious page, while OpenAI removed one fake ChatGPT version but another was later found. This matters because the scam uses familiar services such as ChatGPT, Google, and Cloudflare to appear trustworthy and persuade people to infect their own devices.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This reports an active malware campaign that abuses sponsored Google results and OpenAI-hosted custom GPTs to deliver a RAT through ClickFix lures. It has broad relevance because it uses trusted services to increase credibility and includes concrete persistence and process-monitoring detection indicators.

Signal adds encypted local backup support to iOS, desktop apps

Signal 8.30 completes the rollout of encrypted backups across Android, iOS, and desktop, adding unrestricted local backups and cross-platform backup compatibility. Users must protect their recovery keys, as a local backup key can decrypt all backup files it has encrypted.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Signal version 8.30 completes the rollout of secure backups across Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, and Windows.
  • 02Signal offers encrypted hosted backups with free and paid storage options, as well as unrestricted on-device local backups.
  • 03Both backup methods require a recovery key, and Signal says a local backup recovery key can decrypt all past backup files encrypted with it.
  • 04The update adds local backups to iOS and desktop apps and changes Android backups to the same cross-platform format.
  • 05Signal 8.30 also enables direct iPhone-to-iPhone transfers through a local encrypted Wi-Fi Aware connection.

Signal released version 8.30, completing the rollout of its secure backup feature across Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, and Windows. The update adds on-device local backups to iOS and desktop clients, while Android backups now use the same cross-platform format. The backups allow users to restore chats on another device if they lose their phone.

Signal offers encrypted hosted backups and unrestricted local backups. Both require a recovery key, and Signal says a local recovery key can decrypt all past backup files created with it, making the key a target that threat actors have already sought. Hosted backups also use an additional daily rotating key inside a Trusted Execution Environment, while messages set to disappear within 24 hours are excluded from both backup types.

  • A local backup recovery key has especially high value because it can decrypt every past backup file encrypted with that key, regardless of where those files are stored.
  • Hosted backups add a second key that rotates daily in a protected environment, providing additional protection and forward secrecy that the article does not attribute to local backups.
  • Signal excludes disappearing messages set to vanish within 24 hours from both backup methods, limiting what can be preserved in an archive.
  • Attackers began targeting Signal backup recovery keys shortly after the secure backup feature was introduced.

Signal has expanded its chat backup feature to iPhones and desktop computers, so people can save and restore their conversations if they lose a phone. The backups are locked with a recovery key, but anyone who gets that key could read all of the backup files it unlocks, and attackers have already begun seeking these keys. This matters to Signal users because keeping the recovery key private is essential to protecting saved chats and media.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

Signal 8.30 is a concrete cross-platform secure-backup release with implications for users who store sensitive chat histories. The article highlights that local recovery keys can decrypt all prior backups and have already become a target for threat actors, but it does not describe a new active compromise or urgent vulnerability.

Hackers exploit Citrix NetScaler zero-day to deploy web shells

Attackers are actively exploiting two Citrix NetScaler zero-days, including CVE-2026-88772, to gain root access, deploy WHIPSHOT and SLAPSHOT web-shell/tunneling malware, steal credentials, and pivot into internal networks. Organizations should immediately apply Citrix’s latest updates and inspect appliances for web-server configuration changes, suspicious files, and modified /bin/sh permissions.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Citrix disclosed two actively exploited NetScaler zero-days, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, and released security updates for them.
  • 02Mandiant reported that exploitation of CVE-2026-88772 can bypass authentication, crash the NetScaler Packet Processing Engine, and give attackers root-level access to the underlying FreeBSD system.
  • 03Attackers installed PHP web shells and altered NetScaler web-server settings so files appearing to be CSS, image, Debian package, or signature files could run attacker commands.
  • 04Mandiant identified WHIPSHOT, a PHP web shell and proxy, and SLAPSHOT, a Python-based tunneling tool used to connect compromised NetScaler appliances to internal devices.
  • 05Citrix says both flaws have been exploited, and Mandiant states that installing the latest NetScaler security updates is the only way to address both vulnerabilities.

Attackers are actively exploiting two Citrix NetScaler zero-days, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, to compromise NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances. Mandiant says activity began by at least early September and affected organizations in North America and Europe across government, financial services, education, legal, and professional-services sectors. Citrix confirmed exploitation of both flaws and released security updates.

Mandiant reports that CVE-2026-88772 can bypass authentication and crash the NetScaler Packet Processing Engine, providing attackers root-level access on the underlying FreeBSD platform. Attackers deployed PHP web shells, changed web-server settings to disguise malicious requests as CSS, image, Debian package, or signature files, and modified /bin/sh permissions to preserve root-level command execution. The campaign also used WHIPSHOT, a PHP web shell and proxy, and SLAPSHOT, a Python tunneling tool that can connect the compromised appliance to internal devices for reconnaissance and credential theft.

Citrix and Mandiant recommend installing the latest NetScaler security updates, which Mandiant says is the only way to address both vulnerabilities. Organizations should inspect appliances for unauthorized PHP handlers or aliases in httpd.conf, suspicious .deb or .sig files containing PHP, modified /bin/sh permissions, unusual NSPPE crashes, and files associated with SLAPSHOT. Disabling DTLS or blocking inbound UDP/443 may mitigate CVE-2026-88772 when DTLS is not needed, but does not protect against CVE-2026-88771.

  • Disabling DTLS or blocking inbound UDP/443 can reduce exposure to CVE-2026-88772 when DTLS is unnecessary, but Citrix states this does not protect against the separately exploited CVE-2026-88771 flaw.
  • Attackers disguised web-shell traffic as ordinary requests for CSS, image, Debian package, or signature files by changing NetScaler web-server configuration, and some web shells returned fake HTTP 404 responses to conceal command execution.
  • Although the initial compromise provided root access, the attackers modified /bin/sh with the setuid permission so commands sent through their web shells would continue to run with root-level privileges.
  • SLAPSHOT can remove itself after idle periods, while WHIPSHOT can check whether it is running and relaunch embedded Python payloads, making its presence harder to identify.
  • GreyNoise detected an attempted exploitation event on September 24, three days before Citrix publicly disclosed the two vulnerabilities.

Hackers are using two newly discovered flaws in Citrix NetScaler systems, which many organizations use to provide remote access and connect to internal services, to take control of those systems. The attacks have affected or targeted organizations in North America and Europe, including government, financial, education, legal, and professional-services groups. Once inside, attackers can hide command tools, steal login details, and use the compromised system as a bridge into the organization’s internal network. Citrix has released fixes, and installing them is the only way to fully protect against both flaws.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a must-read report on active zero-day exploitation of widely deployed Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances. The attacks provide root access, enable web-shell persistence and internal-network tunneling, and affect two flaws for which patching is the only complete mitigation.

Apple patches CoreGraphics zero-day flaw exploited in attacks

Apple patched an actively exploited CoreGraphics out-of-bounds write zero-day that could allow arbitrary code execution through malicious files in highly targeted attacks. Users should update affected iPhones, iPads, and Macs to iOS/iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, or macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 promptly.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Apple released security updates for an out-of-bounds write flaw in CoreGraphics that can allow arbitrary code execution when a maliciously crafted file is processed.
  • 02Apple said the flaw may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals using iOS versions before iOS 27.
  • 03The issue was discovered by Meta Product Security and has been addressed through improved bounds checking in iOS 26.7.1, iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1.
  • 04Affected devices include iPhone 11 and later, several iPad models, and Macs running macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 or Tahoe 26.7.1.
  • 05Apple strongly advised users to install the security updates promptly, despite the reported exploitation appearing limited to highly targeted attacks.

Apple released security updates for a CoreGraphics zero-day flaw that it says may have been used in an “extremely sophisticated” attack against specific targeted individuals using versions of iOS before iOS 27. Meta Product Security discovered the issue, which is an out-of-bounds write weakness in CoreGraphics, Apple’s framework for graphics, image rendering, and text drawing. Apple said processing a maliciously crafted file could lead to arbitrary code execution.

The flaw affects a broad range of iPhone and iPad models, as well as Macs running macOS Sequoia and macOS Tahoe. Apple addressed it with improved bounds checking in iOS 26.7.1, iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1. Although the reported exploitation appears limited to highly targeted attacks, the article advises users to install the updates promptly to reduce the risk of potential ongoing attacks.

  • The risk is not limited to one Apple device type because CoreGraphics is used across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, and tvOS, although the listed fixes in the article cover iPhone, iPad, and Mac platforms.
  • A specially crafted file is the stated trigger, meaning the issue can arise when affected software processes content rather than requiring a physical attacker to be nearby.
  • Apple characterized the reported use as aimed at specific individuals, but the broad list of supported iPhone, iPad, and Mac models means a wide range of users can apply the available fixes.
  • The article says this is Apple’s second zero-day fixed since the start of the year and notes that seven actively exploited zero-days were fixed last year, highlighting repeated in-the-wild patching activity.

Apple released updates to fix a security flaw in software used to display images, graphics, and text on iPhones, iPads, and Macs. The company says the flaw may already have been used in very sophisticated attacks aimed at specific people, where opening a specially made file could let an attacker run their own code on the device. Many newer and older Apple devices are affected, so installing the latest iOS, iPadOS, or macOS updates is important to reduce the risk of ongoing targeted attacks.

New Spectre v2 attack variant leaks Linux root password hash in minutes

Researchers disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a Spectre v2 variant that can exploit stale CPU branch-prediction data after JIT code reuse to leak a Linux root password hash in minutes. The issue affects tested Intel, AMD, and Arm CPUs; Linux kernel fixes are available, so users should update their OS and firmware.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Researchers at VUsec and Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a Spectre v2 variant that exploits stale branch-prediction information after JIT-generated code is reused at the same memory address.
  • 02In Linux tests, unprivileged classic BPF programs were used to leak a running su process's root password hash at eight bytes per second, recovering it in an average of three minutes on Raptor Cove and five minutes on Lion Cove.
  • 03The researchers demonstrated Linux cBPF exploits both under the default configuration and with constant blinding enabled.
  • 04VUsec confirmed the relevant behavior on every tested Intel, AMD, and Arm CPU, stating that current CPUs lack a mechanism to synchronize branch predictions with changed code.
  • 05The reported issues are tracked as CVE-2026-64507 and CVE-2026-64508, and fixes have been merged into the Linux kernel.

Researchers at VUsec and Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a new Spectre v2 variant that can recover Linux root password hashes in minutes. BTR takes advantage of stale information in a processor component that predicts where code will jump next after a just-in-time engine frees code and reuses its memory address for different code. The researchers said this demonstrates that attacks involving dynamically changed code are practical, contrary to an assumption in the field since 2018.

In Linux tests, unprivileged classic BPF programs trained an old prediction, then triggered speculative execution of attacker-crafted replacement code at a misaligned location. The resulting cache traces allowed data to be inferred byte by byte, with a running su process’s root password hash leaked at eight bytes per second; end-to-end tests recovered it in three minutes on Raptor Cove and five minutes on Lion Cove on average. The behavior was confirmed on tested Intel, AMD, and Arm CPUs, while Linux fixes for CVE-2026-64507 and CVE-2026-64508 have been merged into the kernel; users are advised to apply operating-system and firmware updates.

  • BTR challenges the assumption held since 2018 that attacks based on dynamically changing code were impractical in real-world JIT engines.
  • Linux’s constant blinding hardening did not prevent the demonstrated cBPF exploit, because the researchers adapted it to place attacker-controlled instructions in jump offsets.
  • Recovering a password hash does not directly reveal the password, but the hash can be cracked offline or with cloud resources depending on the password strength and hashing algorithm.
  • The researchers observed stale predictions in Firefox’s SpiderMonkey and a speculative sandbox-check bypass path in GraalVM, but did not complete end-to-end browser or GraalVM attacks in their experiments.

Researchers found a new weakness called Branch Target Reuse that can make a computer briefly follow old, incorrect instructions and reveal protected information. In tests, it let an unprivileged user on Linux recover the root account’s password hash—a scrambled form of the password—in as little as a few minutes. The behavior was confirmed on tested Intel, AMD, and Arm processors, and an attacker might try to crack a stolen hash to obtain the real password. Linux fixes are available, so users should install current operating-system and firmware updates.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a concrete new Spectre v2 research finding with broad relevance to Linux systems and tested Intel, AMD, and Arm CPUs. It demonstrates root password-hash leakage in minutes and has Linux kernel fixes available, although the article does not report active exploitation in the wild.

Automated AI agent used to breach cybersecurity nonprofit DIVD

Dutch vulnerability-disclosure nonprofit DIVD says attackers exploited an undisclosed technical flaw and used an autonomous AI agent for noisy, error-prone post-exploitation activity. The organization is investigating, has notified Dutch authorities, and plans to disclose more details after assessing other potential victims.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) said it was breached through an undisclosed technical vulnerability that was not Citrix NetScaler.
  • 02DIVD said the intruder used an automated AI agent for post-compromise activity, with the agent choosing its next actions autonomously.
  • 03The organization described the activity as loud, messy, and error-prone, including the agent interfering with its own attempt to intercept communications through password spraying.
  • 04DIVD said the attacker’s purpose and the incident’s impact remain unclear while its investigation continues.
  • 05DIVD notified police, the Dutch data-protection authority, and the National Cyber Security Center, and plans a more detailed update on October 1.

The Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD), a nonprofit that identifies and reports internet-exposed known vulnerabilities, said it was breached after seven years of uneventful operations. DIVD said the intrusion exploited an undisclosed technical vulnerability in a system that was not Citrix NetScaler. The organization described the incident as an agentic AI-powered attack, though the attacker’s purpose and the resulting impact remain unclear.

According to DIVD, an automated AI agent conducted post-exploitation activity on its network, choosing its own next steps and leaving extensive evidence through its actions and comments. DIVD said the agent operated at high speed with sloppy logic, made “pretty dumb” mistakes, and interfered with its own adversary-in-the-middle effort through password spraying. DIVD has notified police, the Dutch data-protection authority, and the National Cyber Security Center, and says it will provide a fuller update on October 1 while notifying other possible victims of the same flaw when possible.

  • DIVD said the AI agent over-explained its decisions in comments and left enough evidence for researchers to reverse-engineer much of the incident.
  • The agent’s autonomous behavior did not make it effective: DIVD said it used sloppy logic, performed “pretty dumb” actions, and disrupted its own attempt to intercept communications.
  • DIVD’s plan to notify other possible victims indicates the undisclosed technical flaw may affect systems beyond the organization itself.

The Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure, a nonprofit that helps organizations find and fix known software weaknesses, says someone broke into one of its systems by taking advantage of an undisclosed flaw. The intruder reportedly used an AI program that chose its own next actions, but it made mistakes and left behind a lot of evidence. The full purpose and impact are still unknown, and DIVD is working with Dutch authorities while checking whether others may be exposed to the same software weakness.

Here We Go Again (Citrix NetScaler DTLS Preauth Memory Overflow CVE-2026-88772)

Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88772 is an actively exploited, pre-authentication DTLS memory overflow that can enable remote code execution on VPN gateways with DTLS enabled by default. Organizations should urgently update NetScaler ADC/Gateway to Citrix’s fixed releases or disable DTLS where feasible.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-88772 is a Citrix NetScaler DTLS memory overflow that Citrix says was exploited in the wild as a zero-day and can lead to remote code execution or denial of service.
  • 02The issue affects NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway when DTLS is enabled, which the article states is the default configuration for VPN virtual servers.
  • 03The vulnerable NSPPE code reassembles attacker-controlled DTLS fragments and copies an oversized chain of NetScaler Buffers into a fixed 35,840-byte scratch buffer without sufficient bounds checking.
  • 04The article demonstrates that 120 crafted records can cause approximately 173,665 bytes to be copied, overflowing the scratch buffer by 137,825 bytes.
  • 05Citrix recommends updating to NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.37 or later, 13.1-64.23 or later, and the listed FIPS or NDcPP fixed releases.

Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88772 is a DTLS memory-overflow flaw affecting NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, which Citrix reported as exploited in the wild as a zero-day. It can lead to remote code execution or denial of service when DTLS is enabled, and the article states that DTLS is enabled by default on VPN virtual servers. Citrix addressed it in a bulletin covering eight vulnerabilities and recommends upgrading to the listed fixed releases.

The article’s analysis finds that NetScaler’s DTLS reassembly logic can be tricked into treating 120 large records as one completed 120-byte handshake message. Although each malicious fragment claims to supply only one byte, NetScaler retains almost all of every record in its linked buffer chain and then copies the full chain into a fixed 35,840-byte scratch buffer without checking the total size. The demonstrated payload copies 173,665 bytes, overflowing the buffer by 137,825 bytes; the researchers show how the resulting memory corruption could be used to reach shellcode execution. The patched build adds remaining-space checks before copying each buffer in the chain.

  • Passing the DTLS cookie check does not require a user login; it only proves that the sender can receive packets at its IP address.
  • The crafted records claim to contribute one byte each to a 120-byte message, but NetScaler retains nearly the entire large packet for each fragment, producing a roughly 174 KB reassembly chain.
  • The fixed NetScaler build adds per-buffer remaining-space checks before each copy into the 35,840-byte scratch buffer, directly preventing the oversized-chain condition.
  • The vulnerable nsppe binary has no position-independent execution protection, allowing the researchers to use fixed code addresses in their demonstrated path from memory corruption to code execution.
  • Citrix’s bulletin includes CVE-2026-88778, which requires Enhanced ISN Generation to be enabled and is not fully addressed by upgrading alone.

The article examines a serious flaw in Citrix NetScaler devices, which organizations use to manage application traffic and provide secure remote access. Attackers were already using the flaw before a user signs in, allowing them to send specially crafted network messages that can crash the device or potentially take control of it. Organizations using affected NetScaler ADC or Gateway systems, especially with the default remote-access setting enabled, need to install Citrix’s updates because a compromised gateway can expose systems behind it.

Official MCP Python SDK Flaw Can Let Malicious Servers Steal OAuth Credentials

A high-severity flaw in the official MCP Python SDK could let malicious MCP servers redirect OAuth token exchanges and steal client secrets, authorization codes, and PKCE verifiers. Upgrade to versions 1.30.0 or 2.2.0, configure issuer validation for machine-to-machine OAuth providers, and rotate credentials if untrusted servers may have been contacted.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A malicious MCP server could exploit affected versions of the official MCP Python SDK to obtain OAuth client secrets, authorization codes, and PKCE proof keys during a login flow.
  • 02The issue affects MCP clients using the SDK over HTTP with OAuthClientProvider, ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider, PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider, or the deprecated RFC7523OAuthClientProvider when they connect to servers they do not fully control.
  • 03The SDK was fixed in version 1.30.0 for the 1.x line and version 2.2.0 for the 2.x line, adding checks that reject unexpected login-service details.
  • 04Users of ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider or PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider must also specify issuer= after upgrading, while users of the deprecated RFC7523OAuthClientProvider must migrate because it has no issuer= option.
  • 05Organizations that may have connected to an untrusted MCP server should rotate client secrets, revoke tokens, and clear stored OAuth client registrations after upgrading.

A flaw in the official MCP Python SDK could allow a malicious MCP server to steal OAuth credentials from an application connecting to it. Affected versions could send a client secret, authorization code, and PKCE proof key to an attacker-controlled token endpoint. Cycode demonstrated the exchange in a test and said the resulting access token carries the permissions granted to the application.

The issue affects HTTP-based MCP clients using OAuthClientProvider, ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider, PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider, or the deprecated RFC7523OAuthClientProvider when connecting to servers they do not fully control. MCP servers built with the SDK, local stdio clients, and clients that provide their own tokens are not affected. The fixes are version 1.30.0 on the 1.x line and 2.2.0 on the 2.x line, but users of the two machine-to-machine providers must also set issuer=; organizations that may have connected to an untrusted server should clear registrations, rotate client secrets, and revoke tokens.

  • For machine-to-machine OAuth providers, upgrading alone does not provide protection unless the application also sets issuer= to identify the login service that owns its credentials.
  • The interactive login flow can still appear legitimate to the user because the approval page is the genuine login page even when credentials are ultimately sent to an attacker-controlled endpoint.
  • Existing stored OAuth client registrations must be cleared after upgrading because registrations created by older versions are not bound to a particular login service.
  • On version 1.30.0, the warning about configuring issuer= is a Python deprecation warning that is hidden by default, making the required security change easy to overlook.

A flaw in the official Python software kit for connecting AI apps to outside services could let a fake MCP server steal the login credentials an app uses for a real service. It affects apps that use certain login methods, connect over the web to servers they do not fully control, and hold credentials for another service; locally connected apps and apps that supply their own login tokens are not affected. Stolen credentials could let an attacker obtain access with the same permissions as the app, and long-lasting secrets may keep working until they are changed. Updating the kit and, where needed, naming the expected login service helps prevent this.

This is a high-severity OAuth credential-disclosure flaw in the official MCP Python SDK, with concrete fixes and configuration steps that affected users must apply. New Spectre-v2 BTR Attack Leaks Linux Memory Despite Existing Defenses

Researchers disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a new Spectre-v2 technique that abuses stale indirect-branch predictions in JIT engines to transiently execute reused code locations and leak secrets. Proof-of-concept exploits extracted a root password hash from fully patched Intel Linux systems, prompting Linux kernel mitigations for CVE-2026-64507 and CVE-2026-64508.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Researchers from VUSec and Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a new Spectre-v2 variant affecting JIT engines.
  • 02BTR exploits stale indirect-branch prediction entries that can remain after JIT-generated code is freed and its memory is reused.
  • 03The researchers found SpiderMonkey, GraalVM, and the Linux kernel's cBPF JIT to be affected, with differing exploitability and data-leakage rates.
  • 04Two proof-of-concept Linux kernel exploits recovered a root password hash within minutes from a fully patched Intel system using default protections.
  • 05Linux kernel mitigations for BTR were released and merged as CVE-2026-64507 and CVE-2026-64508.

Researchers from VUSec and Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR), a new Spectre-v2 variant affecting Just-In-Time code engines. The technique was evaluated against Firefox’s SpiderMonkey, GraalVM, and the Linux kernel’s cBPF JIT, with different levels of exploitability and leakage rates. BTR relies on stale CPU branch-prediction information that can persist after generated code is freed and memory is reused.

An attacker able to run unprivileged code in a JIT engine can train a processor to predict a jump to one code region, cause that region to be freed and partly reused, and then trigger a speculative jump to the stale location. This can temporarily redirect execution to an invalid entry point, bypass hardening measures or use misaligned instructions, and reveal sensitive data through cache-state changes. The researchers created two Linux proof-of-concept exploits that recovered a root password hash within minutes from a fully patched Intel system with default protections; Linux mitigations were merged as CVE-2026-64507 and CVE-2026-64508, while GraalVM and Mozilla are pursuing different mitigation approaches.

  • BTR can redirect speculative execution to an old code location after that memory has been freed and reused, creating a temporary form of execute-after-free behavior even though normal program execution remains coherent.
  • The researchers demonstrated that existing default protections on a fully patched Intel Linux system did not prevent recovery of a root password hash within minutes.
  • Mitigation approaches differ by platform: Linux added kernel fixes, GraalVM randomizes JIT code-cache locations to hinder memory-region reuse, and Mozilla is prioritizing site isolation while considering branch-predictor barriers.

Researchers found a new weakness in modern computer processors that can let unprivileged programs briefly access data they should not be able to read. It affects code-generation features used by Firefox, GraalVM, and the Linux operating system; in demonstrations, researchers recovered a Linux system’s root password hash from a fully updated Intel machine. This matters because the flaw can bypass existing safeguards and expose sensitive information, though fixes have been added to the Linux kernel.

This is a concrete new Spectre-v2 research finding with proof-of-concept exploits that extracted a root password hash from fully patched Intel Linux systems using default protections. An attacker used stolen DGFIP staff passwords to access French tax administration systems and extract data through the E-Contact taxpayer messaging tool during June and July. The theft affected slightly more than 350,000 individuals and 250,000 businesses, although taxpayers’ own impots.gouv.fr account passwords were not compromised. Data potentially exposed for individuals included tax IDs, contact details, family situations, reference taxable income, withholding rates, and message lists; some message contents may also have been taken.

ANSSI found that the intrusion succeeded because some portals accepted passwords alone, sensitive DGFIP applications were insufficiently separated on the government network, and monitoring did not cover ADER. The DGFIP SOC reset compromised passwords but did not terminate active ADER sessions, allowing one automated extraction to continue for nearly 16 hours after a reset. The activity was not identified until the attacker claimed the theft on August 12, seven weeks after the first data was taken. ANSSI recommended stronger multi-factor authentication, revoking sessions after password resets, monitoring all business applications, detecting unusual data volumes, and preventing personal devices from accessing work resources.

  • The attacker did not need privileged accounts: ordinary DGFIP staff accounts could access large amounts of taxpayer data, highlighting the impact of broad access rights.
  • Multiple warning signs existed but were not connected, including nighttime logins, VPN use, Indian or known-malicious IP addresses, suspicious searches, and 11 GB of data exchanged.
  • ANSSI’s network-level sensors could not detect the misuse of legitimate staff accounts because the agency lacked access to application logs, demonstrating the detection gap between network monitoring and application activity.
  • The APEX portal’s email-delivered one-time code could be bypassed if the attacker had access to the same mailbox, which is why ANSSI recommended stronger second factors such as hardware tokens or authenticator apps.

Someone used stolen passwords belonging to French tax staff to access government systems and copy tax-related information on more than 350,000 people and 250,000 businesses. The exposed information could include names and contact details, tax identifiers, family details, income information, and records of messages sent to the tax office, although taxpayers’ own account passwords were not taken. The activity went unnoticed for seven weeks because the systems did not require an extra sign-in check in some places and did not adequately track unusual data collection. The incident shows how a single stolen work password can put large numbers of citizens and businesses at risk when government systems are not designed to detect and stop misuse quickly.

A phishing email spoofing a privately held UK industrial firm’s own domain arrived from an unauthorized external IP and failed reverse-DNS, SPF, and DMARC checks at a hosted filtering relay. Despite those failures, the relay recorded the message as whitelisted with sender as its evidence and recommended that it be accepted. The article does not establish why the relay allowed it, but notes that the authentication results and acceptance decision appeared together without being reconciled.

The message was then re-injected through the organization’s on-premises Exchange 2019 server and outbound host before reaching Microsoft 365. Because the final sending host was authorized for the organization’s domain, Microsoft 365 recorded SPF and DMARC passes, marked composite authentication as passing, assigned SCL:-1, and classified the message as internal; the message had no DKIM signature. Four mailboxes received a fake DocuSign lure within six minutes, with the working link using the emj.to shortener and the campaign labeled by IRONSCALES as credential theft. The forged domain had produced 39 incidents since March 2025, including 37 automatically resolved as malicious and one human malicious verdict, with no safe verdicts recorded.

  • The hosted relay’s authentication findings and its allow decision were recorded together, showing that its reputation stage accepted a sender identity that the relay’s own earlier checks had rejected.
  • Microsoft 365’s final SPF and DMARC passes reflected the organization’s authorized outbound host after re-injection rather than the external origin, while the message had no DKIM signature.
  • The message’s internal classification excluded it from external-sender tagging even though its original source was an unauthorized external IP address.
  • The phishing kit exposed repeatable detection clues outside authentication: it copied each recipient’s Message-ID into the visible subject and a fake PDF filename, used a non-rendering logo reference, and included a claimed Access Documents button that did not exist.
  • The 39-incident history for the forged domain, including no safe verdicts or release requests, provides evidence of repeated malicious use rather than an isolated authentication-routing failure.

A criminal email pretending to come from a UK industrial company’s own address was initially recognized as suspicious, but a filtering service still let it through. After the company’s own email servers forwarded it onward, Microsoft 365 treated it as an internal message and delivered a fake DocuSign notice designed to steal login details from four employees. This matters because a message can appear trustworthy after passing through familiar systems even when earlier checks correctly identified that it was forged, putting organizations at risk of account theft.

Unit 42 examined Kubernetes operators, automated components that manage custom resources in a cluster, and found that their highly privileged service accounts can create serious security weaknesses. The researchers released OperTraitor, an open-source LLM-powered analysis tool that compares an operator’s documented purpose with the permissions it actually receives and gives it a risk score from 1 to 10. Their review found that slightly more than 5% of operators requested excessive privileges, while outdated or abandoned versions can remain easily available through OperatorHub and the Operator Lifecycle Manager.

One case involved IBM Turbonomic’s Prometurbo operator, which had cluster-wide permission to read secrets, potentially exposing service-account tokens, database credentials, API keys and TLS certificates from unrelated namespaces if the operator were compromised. IBM addressed the issue and published CVE-2026-6389 with a CVSS score of 8.8. The article also found broad permissions in the Datadog operator, and Datadog documented why user-defined secret names complicated narrower permissions and described its mitigations. Unit 42 warns that AI-enhanced and agentic operators could increase the consequences of excessive permissions, and recommends verifying operator sources, limiting permissions and namespaces, auditing manifests, monitoring service-account activity, and applying strict network controls to AI-enabled operators.

  • AI-enhanced operators can turn broad permissions into a more serious risk because an operator connected to an external AI system could provide that system with unchecked access to cluster resources.

The article warns that automated helper programs used to run Kubernetes computer environments are often given far more access than they need, so a hacked helper could expose passwords, secret keys, and other sensitive information across an entire organization. The researchers found examples containing personal information, password hashes, private messages, access tokens, MAC addresses, and business data. Mitiga used AWS Lambda Step Functions and boto3 to scan public snapshots, copy them to its own account, restore database instances, extract schemas and table contents, and then remove the instances. The European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) began applying reporting obligations to manufacturers on September 11. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents. The CRA entered into force in mid-December 2024 and is still progressing toward full application in December 2027.

Manufacturers must submit an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of an issue and provide a notification with general information and an initial assessment within 72 hours. Final reports for actively exploited vulnerabilities are due no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure becomes available, while final reports for severe incidents are due within one month after the 72-hour notification. ENISA launched its Single Reporting Platform on September 11 to allow a manufacturer to report once rather than notify each national authority separately.

Reports through the platform are sent to ENISA and the Computer Security Incident Response Team where the manufacturer is based, which normally shares them with other relevant teams. In specified exceptional circumstances, a response team may delay wider sharing when dissemination would create greater cybersecurity risks that cannot be sufficiently controlled. ENISA said the platform is operational but will continue to be improved and expanded based on operational experience and user needs.

  • The final-report deadline for an actively exploited vulnerability is tied to when a corrective or mitigating measure becomes available, rather than simply to when the issue was discovered.
  • The Single Reporting Platform is designed to replace separate notifications to each national authority, with reports sent simultaneously to ENISA and the manufacturer’s national incident-response team.
  • A national incident-response team may delay sharing a report more broadly when disclosure would create greater cybersecurity risks that cannot be controlled through handling restrictions, provided additional specified conditions are met.
  • Although the reporting platform is operational, ENISA states that it plans to expand and improve its functions over the coming months based on operational experience and user needs.

The European Union has started requiring companies that make connected or software-based products to quickly report serious security problems and flaws that criminals are already using. Starting September 11, these companies must send an initial warning within 24 hours and provide further details through a new reporting website run by the EU cybersecurity agency ENISA. This matters because sharing information quickly can help authorities and other affected groups respond before a security problem causes wider harm, while the EU prepares to fully apply these rules in December 2027.

Errol Weiss, chief security officer at Health-ISAC, said this subsidized access could deliver essential security capabilities to hospitals and healthcare organizations at the “last mile,” where they are needed most.

  • The initiative is aimed at small security teams, indicating that the subsidized access and training are intended to address resource constraints among organizations operating essential services.
  • Its planned uses span finding software weaknesses, identifying suspicious activity, and containing harmful actions after access is gained, rather than focusing on only one stage of a security incident.
  • Health-ISAC’s Errol Weiss highlighted hospitals and healthcare organizations as potential beneficiaries, describing subsidized access as a way to bring security capabilities to the operational “last mile.”

OpenAI said it will commit $1 billion in discounted access and training to help small technology security teams protect essential services such as electricity, water, and local government. The program is intended to help teams find serious weaknesses, spot unusual activity, and stop harmful actions if criminals get into their systems. This matters because disruptions to these services can affect communities, while hospitals and healthcare organizations may also gain security help where resources are limited.

OpenAI’s $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders commitment is a concrete industry announcement that could affect small security teams protecting electricity, water, local government, and healthcare services. It does not describe an active incident, exploited flaw, or immediately actionable technical threat.

A classical signature chain is a certificate chain that uses traditional digital-signature algorithms rather than post-quantum ones.
classification concept
Classification is the act of sorting data, events, or systems into categories so they can be handled appropriately.
clickfix

ClickFix lures technique
ClickFix lures are social-engineering tricks that persuade users to copy and run commands by pretending to fix a computer or browser problem.
Client Secret concept
A client secret is a private value an application uses like a password to prove its identity to another service.
ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider tool
A software component that uses the OAuth client-credentials method to let one service authenticate to another service.
ClientTLSKeyExchangeGroup other
ClientTLSKeyExchangeGroup is a log field that records the cryptographic key-exchange algorithm used by a client connection.
Clop threat-actor
Clop is a ransomware group and malware family known for stealing data and extorting victims.
Clop group threat-actor
The Clop group is a cybercriminal ransomware gang known for stealing data and extorting organizations.
cloud concept
The cloud is internet-based computing where data and applications run on remote servers instead of only on your own device.
cloud account concept
A cloud account is an account used to access and manage computing resources such as servers, storage, and databases from a cloud provider.
Cloud accounts concept
Cloud accounts are identities or subscriptions used to access services hosted by providers like AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud.
Cloud credentials concept
Cloud credentials are passwords, keys, or tokens used to access cloud services and resources.
also: node's cloud credentials
cloud environments concept
Cloud environments are computing systems and services run in cloud platforms rather than on local machines.
cloud metadata concept
Cloud metadata is information about cloud resources, such as instance settings or credentials, that cloud services make available to systems.
Cloud proxies tool
Cloud proxies are cloud-hosted services that relay, filter, or inspect traffic between users and online services.
cloud resources concept
Cloud resources are computing services like servers, storage, databases, or apps that run in an internet-hosted cloud environment.
cloud services concept
Computing resources—like storage, apps, and networking—delivered over the internet by providers such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
Cloud Software Group organization
The software company that owns Citrix and its NetScaler product line.
cloudflare
Cloudflare is a company that provides content delivery, DDoS protection, DNS, and web security services.
Cloudflare R2 product
Cloudflare R2 is an object-storage service for storing files and other large data.
Cloudflare Tunnel product
Cloudflare Tunnel is a Cloudflare service that lets a server be reached through Cloudflare without opening inbound ports directly to the internet.
Cloudflare WAF product
Cloudflare WAF is Cloudflare's web application firewall that helps block malicious web traffic before it reaches a website.
Cloudflare Workflows product
Cloudflare Workflows is a Cloudflare service for running multi-step automated processes with saved progress and retries.
Cloudforce One organization
Cloudforce One is Cloudflare's threat intelligence and security research team.
CloudTrail product
CloudTrail is an AWS service that records management API activity.
cluster concept
A group of connected computers or appliances that work together as one system.
cluster admin concept
A cluster admin is a highly privileged role that can manage an entire computing cluster, such as a Kubernetes cluster.
also: cluster administrator, cluster admin across clusters
Cluster secret concept
A protected piece of sensitive data stored in a computing cluster, often containing passwords, tokens, keys, or other credentials.
also: secrets
co-conspirators threat-actor
Co-conspirators are people who work together with others to plan or commit a crime.
Code Cache concept
A memory area where a program stores generated or recently used machine code for fast reuse.
code execution technique
Code execution means an attacker can make a computer or server run commands or software of their choosing.
Code paths concept
Code paths are the different routes a program can take through its instructions depending on inputs and conditions.
Code repositories concept
Code repositories are storage locations where software source code and its change history are kept.
codex
Codex is an OpenAI AI coding model or coding assistant technology for helping write and understand code.
Cold Installs concept
Software installation tests performed without previously downloaded packages or cached setup data.
COLDRIVER threat-actor
COLDRIVER is a Russian-linked threat actor known for phishing and credential-theft campaigns against high-profile targets.
Collaboration concept
Collaboration means people or organizations working together, often by sharing information, systems, or responsibilities.
command execution technique
Command execution means making a computer or device run instructions, often through a shell or remote interface.
command-and-control concept
Command-and-control is the way attackers remotely send instructions to malware and receive data back from infected machines.
also: C2 server, command-and-control (C2) server
Command-and-control server concept
Remote computers controlled by attackers that send orders to infected devices and collect stolen data.
commercial spyware malware
Commercial spyware is surveillance software sold by companies and used to secretly monitor devices or people.
commit concept
A saved set of changes in a version-control system such as Git.
Compatibility Validation concept
Testing and checking that software, hardware, and updates work correctly together.
COMPLETION concept
COMPLETION is a query or event label that generally refers to an autocomplete or completion action.
Composite authentication concept
Composite authentication is using several identity or message-checking signals together to decide whether something is trustworthy.
compression concept
Reducing the size of data or files to save storage or bandwidth, sometimes used to obfuscate malware.
compromise concept
A compromise is a situation where a system, account, or data has been breached or taken over by an attacker.
compromised concept
Compromised means a system, account, or device has been accessed or controlled by someone who should not have access.
compromised account concept
An account whose credentials have been stolen or guessed, allowing an attacker to impersonate the legitimate user.
compromised email accounts concept
Compromised email accounts are email accounts that attackers have gained access to without permission.
Compromised Passwords concept
Compromised passwords are passwords that have been stolen, leaked, guessed, or otherwise exposed to attackers.
compromised-email-account concept
A compromised email account is an email account that an attacker has gained access to and can use without permission.
config.toml concept
config.toml is a configuration file in TOML format that software can use to store settings.
configuration changes concept
Configuration changes are modifications to settings that affect how a system, application, or device behaves.
Configuration file concept
A configuration file is a file that stores settings telling software how to run.
configuration files concept
Configuration files are files that store settings telling software or systems how to behave.
Confirmed Breach concept
A verified incident in which an unauthorized party accessed, stole, exposed, or altered protected information or systems.
Connected Applications concept
Applications that have been linked to an account or service so they can access data or perform actions.
Connected apps concept
Connected apps are third-party applications linked to an account or platform so they can access data or perform actions.
Connecting concept
Connecting is a status meaning a device, app, or service is trying to establish a network connection.
Consent concept
A person's informed agreement to let an organization collect, use, or share their information.
conspiracy concept
Conspiracy is an agreement between people to commit an unlawful act.
Constant Blinding technique
A software hardening technique that changes fixed values in generated code to make some attacks harder.
Contact Details concept
Information used to contact a person, such as an address, email address, or phone number.
container escape technique
A container escape is when an attacker breaks out of an isolated software container to access the underlying host system.
containment technique
Containment is the process of limiting a cyber incident so attackers or malware cannot spread further.
Contextualize technique
Contextualize means to add background and meaning so a security finding can be understood and prioritized.
continuous concept
In security, continuous means something is monitored or updated all the time instead of only during occasional checks.
continuous monitoring concept
Continuous monitoring means constantly watching systems, accounts, or networks for problems or suspicious activity.
Controlled endpoint concept
A controlled endpoint is a server, device, or URL that a tester or attacker controls and can monitor or change.
cookies concept
Cookies are small pieces of data websites store in a browser to remember logins, settings, or tracking information.
cooldown concept
A cooldown is a waiting period before something can happen again.
copy event concept
A copy event is a browser signal that happens when a user copies text or other content from a web page.
CoreGraphics product
An Apple software framework that applications use to draw graphics and handle visual content.
Corporate information monitoring concept
Corporate information monitoring is the practice of watching public and external sources for leaked, exposed, or risky company information.
also: corporate information
correlation concept
Correlation means finding connections between separate events, data points, or alerts that may be related.
also: correlation stack
court documents other
Court documents are official records filed in a legal case.
Cozy Bear threat-actor
A widely reported Russia-linked threat-actor group, also known as APT29.
cPanel product
A web-hosting control panel used to manage websites, email, domains, and server accounts.
CPU concept
A CPU is the main processor in a computer that runs instructions and performs calculations.
crafted file technique
A crafted file is a specially made file designed to trigger a bug, exploit a weakness, or test how software handles unusual input.
credential concept
A credential is proof of identity for logging in, such as a password, security token, API key, or certificate.
credential theft technique
Credential theft is the stealing of usernames, passwords, tokens, or other login information.
credential-harvesting
Credential harvesting is collecting usernames, passwords, or login tokens from victims.
credential-phishing
Credential phishing is a scam that tricks people into entering usernames, passwords, or codes into a fake login page.
credentials concept
Credentials are login details or access tokens that prove a user or system is allowed to access something.
criminal hackers threat-actor
Criminal hackers are people who break into computer systems illegally to steal, extort, disrupt, or otherwise profit.
Criminal Organization concept
A criminal organization is a group of people working together to commit crimes for profit or influence.
critical security vulnerability vulnerability
A critical security vulnerability is a very serious software weakness that could let attackers cause major harm if it is exploited.
Critical Software concept
Software that is important enough that failures or compromise could seriously affect an organization or service.
critical vulnerabilities vulnerability
Critical vulnerabilities are very serious security flaws that could let attackers cause major damage or gain major access.
also: critical weaknesses
Critical vulnerability vulnerability
A critical vulnerability is a very serious security flaw that can cause major damage if exploited.
cross-site scripting vulnerability
Cross-site scripting is a website vulnerability that lets attackers run malicious scripts in other users’ browsers.
cryptocurrency concept
Cryptocurrency is digital money, such as Bitcoin, that uses cryptography and usually runs on a blockchain.
cryptocurrency mining operations concept
Cryptocurrency mining operations use computing power to help run a cryptocurrency network and earn coins as a reward.
cryptocurrency scam concept
A fraud scheme that uses cryptocurrency as bait or for payment, including fake investments, Ponzi schemes, and wallet drains.
Cryptocurrency Transfers concept
Cryptocurrency transfers are movements of digital money such as Bitcoin or Ethereum between online wallets.
cryptocurrency wallet product
A cryptocurrency wallet is software or hardware used to store and use the keys that control digital coins.
cryptocurrency wallets product
Cryptocurrency wallets are tools used to store and manage access to digital currency funds.
Cryptography concept
Cryptography is the use of mathematical methods to protect information from being read or changed by unauthorized people.
cryptojacking technique
Cryptojacking is when attackers secretly use someone else’s computer power to mine cryptocurrency.
CryptoLabe tool
CryptoLabe is Cloudflare's internal AI-assisted tool for finding cryptography in code and planning post-quantum upgrades.
CSS protocol
CSS is the web language used to control how pages look, including colors, fonts, and layout.
cursor
Cursor is an AI-assisted code editor built for software developers.
Custom GPT concept
A custom GPT is a version of an AI chatbot configured for a particular task, set of instructions, or knowledge source.
customer data concept
Customer data is information a company keeps about its customers, such as names, contact details, or purchase history.
customer information concept
Customer information is data a business keeps about its customers, such as names, contact details, purchases, or account records.
Customer Names concept
Names that identify customers and may be sensitive when exposed in a data breach.
Customer Zero concept
Customer Zero is the first known customer or victim affected in an incident or investigation.
CVE vulnerability

CVE identifier concept
A CVE identifier is the standard public tracking number assigned to a known cybersecurity vulnerability.
CVSS score concept
A CVSS score is a standard number used to show how severe a software vulnerability is.
Cyber defense concept
Cyber defense is the work of protecting computers, networks, and data from digital attacks.
Cyber Resilience Act concept
The Cyber Resilience Act is a European Union law aimed at making connected products and software more secure throughout their life cycle.
cyberattack concept
A cyberattack is an attempt to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems or data.
cyberattacks concept
Malicious activities conducted over computer networks to steal data, disrupt operations, or damage systems.
Cybersecurity concept
Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computers, networks, software, and data from digital attacks or misuse.
Cybersecurity Capabilities concept
The people, tools, processes, and skills an organization uses to protect its computers and data.
also: essential cybersecurity capabilities, security capabilities
cybersecurity researchers organization
Cybersecurity researchers are people who study digital threats, software flaws, and attacks to help protect systems.
Cycode organization
Cycode is a software supply-chain and application security company.
D1 product
Cloudflare D1 is a managed SQL database service for Cloudflare applications.
Dark web concept
The dark web is a part of the internet that requires special tools to access and is often discussed in relation to hidden marketplaces and forums.
DarkSword malware
DarkSword is a named malware family, threat, or cyber tool referenced in security reporting.
also: iPhone exploit kit
dashboard tool
A dashboard is a visual interface where users manage settings and view information in a product.
Data access concept
Data access means the ability to view, use, change, or retrieve information from a system.
Data Access Governance concept
Policies and tools used to control, review, and manage who can access an organization's data.
data access logs concept
Data access logs are records showing when data is read, changed, or otherwise accessed.
Data Boundaries concept
Limits that define what information a user, program, or AI agent is allowed to access or use.
data breach concept
A data breach is an incident where sensitive, private, or protected information is accessed, exposed, or stolen without permission.
Data collection concept
Data collection is the process of gathering information from people, systems, devices, or services for analysis or use.
data exfiltration technique
Data exfiltration is the unauthorized removal or copying of data from a system.
data extraction technique
The process of collecting or pulling information out of a device, system, or data source.
data leakage concept
Data leakage is when sensitive information is exposed or shared outside where it should be, accidentally or maliciously.
data theft concept
Data theft is the stealing of information from a system or service.
data thefts concept
Data theft is the unauthorized taking or copying of information from a person or organization.
data-theft-extortion technique
Data-theft-extortion is when criminals steal information and threaten to publish or sell it unless the victim pays.

Database credentials are usernames, passwords, keys, or tokens used to access a database.
DataBreaches.Net organization
DataBreaches.Net is a news and information website focused on data breaches, privacy incidents, and cybersecurity events.

Datadog is a cloud monitoring and security platform used to watch applications, servers, logs, and other systems.
Datadog operator tool
The Datadog operator is a Kubernetes operator that helps deploy and manage Datadog monitoring components in a cluster.
datasets concept
Datasets are collections of information that researchers or tools analyze to find patterns and evidence.
DataSuckers threat-actor
DataSuckers is a threat-actor group referenced in security reporting.
Dates of birth concept
Dates of birth are personal information that can help identify someone and may be sensitive if exposed.
dating sites concept
Dating sites are online services where people create profiles and communicate to meet romantic or social partners.
daybreak other
Daybreak is a named item referenced in security reporting, but the term alone does not clearly identify whether it is a tool, product, campaign, or other entity.
Daybreak for Frontline Defenders organization
An OpenAI program intended to provide cybersecurity resources, training, and support to organizations protecting essential services.
Debian product
A well-known community-driven Linux distribution famous for its stability and package management system.
deception technique
Deception is tricking a person or system into believing something false, often to gain access or hide activity.
Decrypt technique
Decrypt is a cryptographic operation that turns encrypted data back into readable data when the correct key is used.
Defender product
Defender usually refers to Microsoft Defender, Microsoft’s built-in security and antimalware product line.
defenders concept
Defenders are the people or teams responsible for protecting systems and responding to cyber threats.
delaware
Delaware is a U.S. state often referenced in business, legal, or breach-notification contexts.
denial-of-service
Denial-of-service is an attack that overwhelms a system so legitimate users cannot access it.

Deno is a runtime for running JavaScript and TypeScript programs outside the browser, similar in purpose to Node.js.
Department of Justice organization
The main U.S. federal law enforcement agency responsible for prosecuting federal crimes and upholding justice.
dependencies concept
Dependencies are outside software components or libraries that an application needs in order to work.
dependency concept
A dependency is outside software that an application relies on, which can create risk if that outside component is vulnerable or malicious.
dependency lifecycle scripts technique
Dependency lifecycle scripts are commands that package managers run automatically during steps like install, build, or publish.
deprecation warning concept
A deprecation warning is a software message saying that a feature is outdated and may be removed in a future version.
desktop computers product
Desktop computers are personal computers designed to stay in one place on a desk.
Detect technique
Detect means to identify suspicious or malicious activity in systems, networks, or data.
detection concept
Detection is the process of finding signs of suspicious or malicious activity.

A detection gap is a weakness or blind spot that prevents security tools or teams from noticing certain malicious activity.
detection guidance concept
Detection guidance is advice that helps defenders find signs of suspicious or malicious activity in their systems.
detection rules concept
Detection rules are instructions security tools use to flag suspicious behavior or known attack patterns.
detections concept
Alerts or findings generated by security tools indicating that a potential threat or malicious activity has been identified.
Developer Platform product
Cloudflare's environment for building and operating developer applications and services.
development teams organization
Development teams are groups of people who build and maintain software or products.
device fingerprint technique
A device fingerprint is a set of details about a device or browser that can be used to recognize it later.
Device management concept
Device management is the work of setting up, maintaining, securing, and retiring an organization's computers and mobile devices.
DevOps concept
DevOps is a way of working where software development and IT operations teams collaborate to build, deploy, and run software faster.
DGFiP organization
DGFiP is France’s public finance directorate, the government organization responsible for taxes and public accounting.
also: tax administration, the DGFIP

Digital certificates are electronic credentials that help prove a website, device, or user is who they claim to be.
digital currency concept
Digital currency is money or value that exists electronically rather than as physical cash.
digital wallets product
Digital wallets are apps or services that store payment information, cryptocurrency keys, or other digital assets.
disappearing messages concept
Disappearing messages are messages that automatically delete themselves after a set time.
Disclosure concept
Disclosure is the act of reporting or publishing information about a security issue so it can be understood and fixed.
Discovery technique
Discovery is the attacker activity of learning about a victim’s systems, accounts, and network before taking further action.

DKIM is an email signing method that helps verify that a message was authorized by a domain and was not changed after signing.

A DNS resolver is the service that looks up human-readable website names and finds the internet addresses computers use to connect to them.

DocuSign product
A widely used electronic signature and document management service for secure digital agreements.
Dodo Pizza organization
Dodo Pizza is a Russian pizza restaurant chain.

A weakness that lets an attacker force a system to use an older, less secure security method.

DTLS fragment reassembly is the process of joining pieces of a DTLS handshake message into the original complete message.
Durable Objects product
Cloudflare Durable Objects are stateful serverless components that store and coordinate data for applications.
Dutch authorities organization

The Dutch Data Protection Authority is the Netherlands' regulator responsible for enforcing privacy and data protection laws.
Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure organization
A Dutch organization involved in identifying and responsibly reporting security vulnerabilities.
Dutch National Police organization
The Dutch National Police is the national police force of the Netherlands.
Dutch police organization
Dutch police are the law-enforcement authorities of the Netherlands.
dyld product
A core Apple operating-system component that loads program libraries when applications start.
Dynamic Configuration concept
A set of software settings that can be changed or loaded while a system runs rather than being permanently fixed in its code.
early warning concept
Early warning is advance notice of possible cyber danger before it becomes a confirmed or damaging incident.
EC2 product
Amazon EC2 is Amazon Web Services’ cloud service for renting virtual servers.
EC2 instance product
An EC2 instance is a virtual server running in Amazon Web Services.
EC2 Instance Metadata Service protocol
The EC2 Instance Metadata Service is an AWS feature that lets a cloud server retrieve information and credentials about itself.
Education Ministry organization
An Education Ministry is a government department responsible for education policy and public education services.
also: Education ministry's security team
elastic organization
The company behind Elasticsearch and the Elastic Stack, providing search, observability, and security solutions.
Elastic Cloud Serverless product
A cloud service from Elastic that runs search, observability, and security workloads without the user managing the underlying servers.
Elastic Defend product
Elastic Defend is Elastic’s endpoint security product for detecting, preventing, and investigating threats on computers and servers.
Elastic Security product
Elastic Security is Elastic’s security analytics platform for SIEM, endpoint protection, and threat detection.
Elastic Stack product
Elastic Stack is a set of tools used to collect, search, analyze, and visualize logs and other data.
Elastic Workflows product
Automated sequences of actions within Elastic's security platform that help analysts investigate and respond to threats.
also: Elastic workflow
Electricity concept
Electrical power used by homes, businesses, and essential public services.
also: power
Electricity Sector concept
The industry that generates, transmits, and distributes electrical power.

Elevated means running with higher permissions than a normal user, such as administrator-level access.
elevated permissions concept
Higher-level access rights that let a user or program make important changes to a computer or network.
email access concept
Email access means the ability to read, send, or manage someone’s email account, which attackers often want because it can unlock other services.
email accounts concept
Email accounts are user accounts that let people send, receive, and store email messages.
email addresses concept
Email addresses are the unique names people use to send and receive email, such as user@example.com.

Email security protects inboxes and users from threats such as phishing, malware, and scam messages.

Email spoofing is when an attacker makes an email look like it came from someone else.

emerging threats concept
Emerging threats are new or growing risks that security teams are starting to see and prepare for.

Employee Email Credentials concept
The login information, such as a work email address and password, used to access an employee's email account.
Enablement package product
A small Windows update that turns on features already included in an earlier version.
encrypted concept
Encrypted data has been scrambled so that only someone with the right key can read it.
encrypted data concept
Encrypted data is information that has been scrambled so it cannot be read without the right key.
encryption concept
Encryption is a way of scrambling information so only someone with the right key can read it.
end to end concept
End to end means something is handled across the whole process from start to finish, often without gaps between steps.
endpoint concept
An endpoint is a user device such as a laptop, phone, or server that connects to a network.
also: endpoint’s, host, hosts
endpoint detection and response product
Endpoint detection and response is security software that watches computers and devices for suspicious activity and helps respond to threats.
also: EDR, enterprise-wide endpoint detection and response
endpoint management concept
Endpoint management is the practice of monitoring, configuring, and securing devices such as laptops, desktops, and phones.
endpoints concept
Endpoints are user-facing devices such as laptops, desktops, or phones that connect to systems and data.
engagement concept
Engagement means how often people interact with a website, app, message, or notification.

Enhanced ISN Generation is a network setting that makes TCP connection sequence numbers harder for attackers to predict.
